IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
MISC. APPLICATION NOS. 2689-90 OF 2025
IN
(CRL. APPEAL NOS. 132-133 OF 2017)
THE STATE OF UTTAR           … APPELLANT(S)
PRADESH
              
VERSUS 
AJMAL BEG ETC.                   … RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. This Court  vide judgment dated 15.12.2025
passed  in  State  of  U.P .  v.  Ajmal  Beg
[Criminal Appeal Nos. 132-133 of 2017], while
allowing the said appeals and restoring the
judgment  of  trial  court  convicting  the
appellants under section 304-B and 498-A of
the Indian Penal Code, 1860, (corresponding
Sections 80 and 85 of the Bharatiya Nyaya
Sanhita, 2023) noted that while in this case,
                                       Page 1 of 13

## Page 17

the  accused  person(s)  has  finally  been
brought  to  book,  there  are  many  cases  in
which  it  is  not  happen.  Many,  who  openly
seek and give dowry, go scot-free. It has been
noted  time  and  again,  in  various  judicial
pronouncements that Dowry Prohibition Act,
1961  suffers  from  various  difficulties  in  its
implementation.  This  Court  further,
acknowledged  that  when  it  comes  to  the
giving and taking of dowry in particular, this
practice  unfortunately  has  deep  roots  in
society, hence, it being not a matter of swift
change, a concentrated effort is needed on the
part  of  all  the  involved  parties,  be  it
Legislature,  Judiciary,  law  enforcement
agencies,  civil  society  organizations  etc.
Therefore, to address the systemic delay and
ineffective  implementation  attending
prosecutions  under  Section  304-B  and
Section 498-A, IPC and the Dowry Prohibition
Act, 1961 following directions were issued:
“26. With an intent to further this change, we
issue the following directions: - 
                                       Page 2 of 13

## Page 18

(a) to ensure that the change brought in is able
to make an impact on the efforts to eradicate
this  evil,  it  is  to  be  ensured  that  the  future
generation,  youngsters  of  today,  are  informed
and made aware about this evil practice and the
necessity to eschew it. As such, it is directed
that  States  and  even  the  Union  Government
consider  changes  as  are  necessary  to  the
educational curricula across levels, reinforcing
the  constitutional  position  that  parties  to  a
marriage are equal to one another and one is
not subservient to the other as is sought to be
established by giving and taking of money and
or articles at the time of marriage;
(b)  The  law  provides  for  the  appointment  of
Dowry Prohibition Officers40 in States. It is to
be ensured that these officers are duly deputed,
aware  of  their  responsibilities  and  given  the
necessary wherewithal to carry out the duties
entrusted to them. The contact details (name,
official phone number and email ID) of such an
officer  designated  to  this  position  are
disseminated adequately by the local authorities
ensuring awareness of citizens of the area; 
(c)  the  police  officials,  as  also  the  judicial
officers  dealing  with  such  cases,  should
periodically be given training, equipping them to
fully  appreciate  the  social  and  psychological
implications which are often at the forefront of
these  cases.  This  would  also  ensure  a
sensitivity  of  the  concerned  officials  towards
genuine cases versus those which are frivolous
and abusive of the process of law; 
(d)  it  is  not  lost  on  us that  the instant  case
began in 2001 and could only be concluded 24
years later by way of this judgment. It is but
obvious that there would be many such similar
cases. The High Courts are requested to take
stock of the situation, ascertain the number of
cases pending dealing with Section 304-B, 498-
                                       Page 3 of 13

## Page 19

A from the earliest to the latest for expeditious
disposal; and 
(e) in furtherance of (a) above, we also recognize
that many people today are/have been outside
the education fold, and that it is equally, if not
more  so,  important  to  reach  them  and  make
accessible  and  comprehensible,  the  relevant
information regarding the act of giving or taking
of  dowry  as  also  other  acts  sometimes
associated therewith, other times independent
thereof  (mental  and  physical  cruelty)  is  an
offence in law. The District Administration along
with the District Legal Services Authorities, by
engaging and involving civil society groups and
dedicated  social  activists,  is  requested  to
conduct  workshops/awareness  programs  at
regular intervals. This is to ensure change at
the grassroot level. 
27. Let a copy of this judgment be circulated
electronically  to  the  Registrar  General  of  the
High  Courts  who  are  requested  to  place  the
same  before  the  Learned  Chief  Justices  and
solicit directions in accordance with the above,
and also, to the Chief Secretaries of all States
for necessary follow up action. 
27.1 While the main appeals are disposed of, so
far as these directions are concerned, to ensure
compliance  thereof,  as  also  issue  any  other
directions as may be necessary, list this matter
after  four  weeks.  States  are  requested  to  file
affidavits  indicating  the  position  qua  the
direction given under (b) hereinabove. The High
Courts shall do the same for (d).”
2. Pursuant to the aforesaid directions, affidavits
and  data  have  been  filed  by  several  High
Courts, States and Union Territories. We have
heard the learned counsel appearing for the
                                       Page 4 of 13

## Page 20

States and, in particular, Mr. Kunal Chatterji,
learned counsel, who has assisted this Court
by placing on record a consolidated analysis
of  the  affidavits/data  so  filed,  along  with
suggestions  received  from  the  High  Courts,
States  and  Union  Territories,  and  a  set  of
proposed  directions  for  the  consideration  of
this Court.
3. Having considered the material placed before
us  and  the  submissions  advanced,  we  now
proceed to pass the following directions:
i. Strengthening of Institutional Support
Mechanisms: States and Union Territories
shall  ensure  effective  functioning  and
dissemination  of  information  regarding
Dowry  Prohibition  Officers
appointed/designated  under  the  Dowry
Prohibition  Act,  1961,  and  shall
strengthen:
a. One Stop Centres,
b. Family Counselling Centres,
c. Women Help Desks,
                                       Page 5 of 13

## Page 21

d. victim assistance mechanisms,
e. helplines, and
f. online  grievance  redressal  systems  for
facilitating  access  to support and  legal
remedies for aggrieved women.
ii. Awareness and Educational Measures:
States  and  Union  Territories,  in
coordination  with  Departments  of
Education, Women and Child Development
Departments,  State  Legal  Services
Authorities  and  other  appropriate  bodies,
shall undertake sustained awareness and
sensitization programmes concerning:
a. the social evil of dowry,
b. gender equality,
c. constitutional values,
d. and  women's  rights,  including  through
educational  curricula,  awareness
campaigns,  community  outreach
programmes and legal literacy initiatives.
iii. Priority Classification and Monitoring of
Cases: All  Courts  dealing  with  offences
                                       Page 6 of 13

## Page 22

under  Sections  304B  and  498A
IPC/Sections 80 and 85 BNS, 2023 shall,
as far as practicable, treat such matters as
priority  cases  and  endeavour  to  ensure
expeditious  disposal  thereof,  without
adversely  affecting  the  hearing  of  other
categories of cases. The concerned District
Judiciary  shall  identify  cases  pending
beyond  three  years,  particularly  those
pending at the stage of framing of charge or
recording  of  evidence,  and  undertake
periodic  monitoring  thereof  through
monthly or quarterly review mechanisms.
iv. Time-Bound Progression of Trial:  All
Trial  Courts  shall  endeavour,  as  far  as
practicable and subject to compliance with
statutory  safeguards  under  the
CrPC/BNSS, to:
a. secure  prompt  appearance  of  accused
expeditiously after filing of charge-sheet;
b. consider  framing  of  charge  preferably
within  60  to  90  days  from  filing  of
charge-sheet;
                                       Page 7 of 13

## Page 23

c. commence recording of evidence within a
reasonable  period  after  framing  of
charge; and
d. proceed with recording of evidence on a
continuous or day- to-day basis in terms
of Section 309 CrPC/Section 346 BNSS,
2023.
Provided  the  timelines  indicated  herein  may
ordinarily  be  adhered  to  as  directory
benchmarks,  subject  to  exceptional  cases
involving  multiple  accused,  supplementary
charge-sheets, forensic delays, non-availability
of accused, or other reasons to be recorded.
v. Witness Regulation of Adjournments and
Management/Witness Calendar: 
a. Trial  Courts/High  Courts  shall
discourage  unnecessary  adjournments
and  ensure  that  adjournments  are
granted only upon recording reasons in
writing. Where counsel for the accused
repeatedly  remains  absent  without
sufficient  cause,  appropriate  Legal  Aid
Counsel  or  Amicus  Curiae  may  be
                                       Page 8 of 13

## Page 24

appointed to ensure that proceedings are
not unnecessarily delayed. Additionally,
where the Investigating Officer has been
transferred  or  retired,  a  substitute  or
holding  officer  shall  be  nominated
sufficiently  in  advance  to  avoid
adjournments.
b. Immediately after framing of charge, the
Trial  Court  shall  prepare  a  witness
calendar  indicating  dates  for
examination  of  material  witnesses,
service of summons and sequencing of
evidence.  This  will  ensure  structured
witness  management  mechanisms,  as
far  as  practicable,  to  secure  timely
attendance  of  witnesses  and  avoid
repeated  deferment  of  evidence.
Investigating  Officers  shall  ensure
prompt  service  of  summons  and
production of witnesses.
vi. Use  of  Technology  and  Digital
Monitoring: The  High  Courts  shall
                                       Page 9 of 13

## Page 25

endeavour to integrate, within the existing
Courts Dashboards/CIS infrastructure: 
a. stage-wise pendency tracking,
b. digital dashboards,
c. automated  alerts  for  old  pending
matters,
d. and case monitoring systems in respect
of  cases  arising  under  Sections  304B
and 498A IPC/Sections 80 and 85 BNS.
vii. Review of Pending Matters Before High
Courts: All High Courts shall endeavour to
periodically  review  old  pending  criminal
appeals, revisions, petitions under Section
482  CrPC/Section  528  BNSS,  2023  and
bail matters, particularly matters involving
interim stay of trial proceedings, and take
appropriate  steps  for  their  expeditious
listing and disposal. Wherever proceedings
are stayed, such orders may be periodically
reviewed in accordance with law.
viii. Training, Sensitization and Specialized
Prosecution: All  States/Union  Territories
                                       Page 10 of 13

## Page 26

and  Hon'ble  High  Courts  shall  ensure
periodic  training  and  sensitization
programmes for:
a. Judicial Officers.
b. Police Officials,
c. Prosecutors,
d. Protection Officers,
e. Counsellors, and
f. Other stakeholders dealing with dowry-
related  offences,  through  Judicial
Academies,  Police  Training  Institutions
and other appropriate bodies.
States  may  also  endeavour  to  designate
prosecutors  having  experience  and
sensitization  in  offences  against  women  for
conducting prosecutions under Sections 304B
and 498A IPC.
ix. Mediation/Counselling in Appropriate
Matrimonial Disputes:  In  cases  arising
primarily out of  matrimonial discord  and
not involving allegations of death, grievous
physical violence, or other serious offences,
                                       Page 11 of 13

## Page 27

the  concerned  Courts  may,  wherever
permissible  in  law  and  considered
appropriate,  explore  the  possibility  of
mediation  or  counselling  through  duly
mediators/counsellors,  without
compromising the rights of parties or the
seriousness of cognizable offences.
x. Compliance and Periodic Reporting:  All
High Courts and States/Union Territories
shall file status/compliance reports on 15 th
of January, May and September before this
Court  for  consideration  and  further
directions,  if  any,  until  the  pendency  of
cases  under  Sections  304B  and  498A
IPC/corresponding Sections 80 and 85 of
BNS,  2023  and  cases  involving  Dowry
Prohibition  Act  1961  is  substantially
reduced,  indicating,  inter  alia,  the
following:
a. pendency and disposal statistics,
b. stage-wise status of cases,
c. awareness initiatives undertaken,
                                       Page 12 of 13

## Page 28

d. appointment/designation  of  Dowry
Prohibition Officers,
e. training programmes conducted,
f. and measures adopted pursuant to the
present directions.
4. List the cases with compliance-cum-periodic
reports on 15th October, 2026.
5. We appreciate the efforts put in by Mr. Kunal
Chatterji, learned counsel, and learned senior
counsel/counsel appearing for the respective
parties.

O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The appellant herein is a qualified doctor who after
obtaining  post-graduation  degree  in  the  field  of
General  Surgery  from  Madurai  Medical  College  is
undertaking super specialty course (M.Ch.) in Cardiac
Thoracic  Surgery  from  Christian  Medical  College,
Vellore  (for  short  the  College)  i.e.,  the  first
respondent. While he was undertaking the M.Ch. course,
he was assigned the duties of a Senior Resident and
paid stipend therefor.  During this period, a charge-
memo was served upon him by the Management of the
College.  Questioning the disciplinary proceedings on
the ground that he was not an employee of the college,
1

## Page 51

the appellant filed a writ petition before the High
Court of Judicature at Madras 1. The said writ petition
was dismissed against which a special leave petition
was filed, which was disposed of with liberty to take
recourse to appropriate remedy. In consequence, the
appellant filed a writ appeal before the Division Bench
of the High Court.  While the writ appeal was pending,
the disciplinary proceedings culminated and order of
termination was passed.  Consequently, the writ appeal
was disposed of by giving liberty to the appellant to
take recourse to appropriate legal remedy.
3. Aggrieved by the order of termination, the appellant
filed a writ petition before a Single Judge Bench of
the High Court.  The said writ petition was allowed
vide order dated 10.10.2023.
4. The principal ground taken to assail the disciplinary
proceedings and the consequential order was that there
was  no  master-servant  relationship  and,  therefore,
disciplinary action could not have been taken by the
management of the institution. The management contested
those proceedings by claiming that the appellant was
appointed as a Senior Resident, and the letter of
1 High Court.
2

## Page 52

appointment indicated that he would be governed by
Regulations  of  the  college  and,  therefore,  there
existed  a  master-servant  relationship  between  the
college and the appellant. Hence, the disciplinary
proceedings cannot be questioned.
5. The  learned  Single  Judge  while  allowing  the  writ
petition  recorded  a  finding  that  there  exists  no
master-servant relationship. In support of its finding,
the learned Single Judge noticed the specific stand of
the National Medical Commission (in short, NMC) in
their reply-affidavit that in the Post Graduate Medical
Education  Regulations  (PGMER),  2000  there  is  no
provision of termination of MCH course without the
approval of the Regulator. Based on that, it was
concluded that a student cannot be terminated by taking
recourse  to  the  provisions  of  Staff  Service
Regulations/ Rules of the College/University.  In light
of the above conclusion and upon finding that there was
no master-servant relationship between the management
of the college and the appellant, the writ petition was
allowed by declaring the disciplinary proceedings as
null and void.
6. Aggrieved by the order of the learned Single Judge, the
3

## Page 53

management  of  the  institution  (i.e.,  the  first
respondent) preferred an intra court appeal before the
Division Bench of the High Court.
7. The High Court vide impugned order dated 30.04.2025 set
aside the order of the learned Single Judge. However,
the finding returned by the learned Single Judge that
there was no master-servant relationship between the
management of the institution and the appellant was not
disturbed.
8. Aggrieved by the decision of the Division Bench of the
High Court, the present appeal has been filed.
9. The learned counsel for the appellant has submitted
that once it is not in dispute that there is no master-
servant relationship between the appellant and the
respondent, the initiation of disciplinary proceedings
by treating the appellant as an employee of the college
cannot  be  sustained  and  therefore  the  order  of
termination is null and void.
10. Having regard to the aforesaid submission, we had
issued notice to the respondents.  Upon service of
notice, NMC has filed its counter affidavit.  In the
counter affidavit, it is specifically stated that
trainee is not an employee of the College and has no
4

## Page 54

rights of employment. Besides, Post Graduate students
are to be paid remuneration under the provisions of
PGMER, 2000. PGMER, 2000 does not explicitly prescribe
for  suspension,  termination  or  rustication  of  a
postgraduate medical trainee student. It is stated in
the counter affidavit that in this regard National
Medical  Commission  Registered  Medical  Practitioner
(Professional Conduct) Regulations, 2023 were notified
on 02.08.2023, but, vide order dated 23.08.2023, the
National  Medical  Commission  has  placed  the  said
regulations  in  abeyance  and  have  reinstated  the
earlier Indian Medical Council (Professional Conduct,
Etiquette and Ethics) Regulations, 2002 (for short
‘IMC Regulations 2002’). It is NMC’s case in the
counter affidavit that currently IMC Regulations 2002
are  applicable.  In  paragraph  21  of  the  counter
affidavit, Regulation 8 of IMC Regulations, 2002 is
extracted  which  speaks  about  Punishment  and
Disciplinary action. Regulation 8 vests the State
Medical Council with the power to hold disciplinary
proceedings  against  any  medical  practitioner  who
violates  the  code  of  conduct  set  out  in  the
regulations.
5

## Page 55

11. Regulations 8.2 to 8.6, which are reproduced in the
counter affidavit, are extracted herein below:
8.2 It is made clear that any compliant
with regard to professional misconduct can
be brought before the appropriate Medical
Council  for  Disciplinary  action.  Upon
receipt of any complaint of professional
misconduct,  the  appropriate  Medical
Council would hold an enquiry and give
opportunity  to  the  registered  medical
practitioner to be heard in person or by
pleader.  If the medical practitioner is
found  to  be  guilty  of  committing
professional misconduct, the appropriate
Medical Council may award such punishment
as deemed necessary or may direct the
removal altogether, or for a specified
period, from the register the name of the
delinquent  registered  practitioner.
Deletion from the Register shall be widely
publicized in local press as well as in
the  publications  of  different  Medical
Associations/ Societies/Bodies.
8.3 In case the punishment of removal from
the register is for a limited period, the
appropriate Council may also direct that
the name so removed shall be restored in
the  register  after  the  expiry  of  the
period for which the name was ordered to
be removed.
8.4  Decision  on  complaint  against
delinquent physician shall be taken within
a time limit of 6 months.
8.5 During the pendency of the complaint
the appropriate Council may restrain the
physician from performing the procedure or
practice which is under scrutiny.
8.6  Professional  incompetence  shall  be
judged by peer group as per guidelines
prescribed by Medical Council of India.”
6

## Page 56

12. As the concurrent finding of the Division Bench as well
as Single Judge of the High Court including the stand
taken by the National Medical Commission is that there
exists  no  master-servant  relationship  between  the
respondent  college  and  the  appellant,  and  those
findings have not been dislodged by the respondent
college, in our view, the college in the event of any
misconduct on the part of the appellant could have had
recourse to the provisions of IMC Regulations, 2002 for
taking such measures as may be permissible in law. On
its  own,  the  respondent  college  could  not  have
terminated the appellant who was undertaking M.Ch.
course therein.  
13. At this stage, the learned counsel for the respondents
has submitted that the Division Bench of the High Court
has taken pains to consider the Committee Report and
various other materials to conclude that the college
was justified in acting against the appellant.  He,
therefore, submits that even if this Court considers
that the action taken by the institution was without
jurisdiction, the matter may be referred to the State
Medical Council to take appropriate proceedings in
7

## Page 57

accordance with the provisions of IMC Regulations, 2002
as has been pointed out in the counter affidavit filed
on behalf of NMC.
14. We  have  accorded  due  consideration  to  the  rival
submissions and have perused the materials placed on
record.  As we find that the learned Single Judge as
well as the Division Bench of the High Court have
concurrently  found  that  there  existed  no  master-
servant relationship between the respondent-college and
the appellant, the disciplinary action taken by the
management of the college against the appellant by
treating  him  as  an  employee  cannot  be  sustained.
However, to address the concerns of the college, it
would be appropriate to give liberty to the respondent-
college to refer the case of the appellant to the State
Medical  Council  for  undertaking  a  disciplinary
proceeding as contemplated under the IMC Regulations,
2002 and take action, if required, in accordance with
law, after giving opportunity of hearing to both sides.
15. Accordingly, we deem it appropriate to allow this
appeal.  The order passed by the Division Bench of the
High Court is set aside and the order passed by the
learned Single Judge is restored. However, we deem it
8

## Page 58

appropriate  to  direct  that  the  management  of  the
respondent-college  will  have  liberty  to  send  the
records of the proceedings undertaken thus far, to the
State Medical Council for taking appropriate action in
accordance with the provisions of IMC Regulations,
2002. If the aforesaid records are transmitted by the
respondent-college to the State Medical Council within
two weeks from today, the State Medical Council shall
issue notice to both sides to submit their response
within next three weeks. Upon receipt of the response,
the State Medical Council shall hold an enquiry in
accordance  with  the  provisions  of  the  applicable
Regulations and, thereafter, if deemed necessary, take
appropriate action/ decision, as may be permissible in
law, after giving due opportunity of hearing to both
sides. It is expected that such decision shall be taken
by the State Medical Council, preferably, within three
months from the date of receipt of written response
from both sides. Till the conclusion of the enquiry by
the State Medical Council, or for a period of four
months from today, whichever is earlier, the appellant
shall remain suspended from the course. The future
course will depend on the decision taken by the State
Medical  Council  albeit  subject  to  the  remedies
9

## Page 59

available to the parties against such decision.
16. The appeal stands allowed in the aforesaid terms.
17. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

(i) Impugned judgment and decree dated 21.12.2021 in 
Special Civil Suit No. 82 of 2018 passed by the learned 3rd 
Additional Senior Civil Judge, Anand, shall remain stayed, 
however, subject to following conditions, 
(a) The appellants of the First Appeal No. 1138 of 2022 - 
original defendants no.2 and 3 deposit total amount of Rs. 
2,54,00,000/- granted by the trial court towards damages to 
the two plaintiffs. 
(b) Appellants of First Appeal No. 1138 of 2022 shall further 
deposit Rs.3,70,000/- towards the cost as per the decree. 
(ii) The original plaintiffs - appellants of First Appeal No. 166 
of 2022 shall be at liberty to withdraw the aforesaid amount. 
(iii) It is however provided that if the appellants of First Appeal 
No. 166 of 2022 exercise the option of withdrawal of the 
amount to be deposited as above, they shall furnish security 
to the satisfaction of the trial court of the amount equivalent to 
the amount which they may withdraw" 
3.6. The appellants-judgment debtors did not comply with 
the direction to deposit the aforesaid amount. 
3.7. The respondent-decree holders sent a reminder dated 
7th February 2023. 
3.8. Thereafter, the respondent -decree holders initiated  
contempt proceedings by filing Civil Application (for 
Breach of Order) No. 1 of 2023 in First Appeal No. 
1138 of 2022 under Order XXXIX Rule 2A of the Code 
of Civil Procedure, 1908 (hereinafter, "CPC"). It was 
prayed, inter alia, that the Court direct the appellants-
judgment debtors to comply with the directions 

## Page 65

CA @ SLP (C) NO. 963/2024  4 
 
contained in paragraph 10 of the order dated 20 th  
December 2022 and hold the appellants guilty of 
disobedience of the same. 
3.9. The High Court, vide order dated 7 th August 2023, 
recorded a prima facie finding of wilful disobedience of 
the directions issued by the High Court and directed 
the appellants-judgment debtors to remain personally 
present before the High Court on 28th August 2023 for 
framing of charge. 
3.10. Aggrieved by the said order, the appellants filed a 
Special Leave Petition before this Court, being SLP (C) 
No. 18338 of 2023. 
3.11. This Court initially stayed the proceedings. However, 
vide order dated 9th October 2023, this Court observed 
that there was no final finding recorded by the High 
Court that the appellants had committed contempt 
and that the appellants could contest the proceedings 
by raising all possible contentions. The appellants 
were also free to apply to the Trial Court for exemption 
from personal appearance. With these observations, 
the SLP was dismissed. 
3.12. Thereafter, the High Court, vide the impugned order, 
again considered the contempt proceedings. The High 
Court held that there was non -compliance with the 
directions issued by it, whereby the appellants -
judgment debtors had been required to deposit the 
aforesaid amount, as well as with the undertaking 

## Page 66

CA @ SLP (C) NO. 963/2024  5 
 
filed by the appellants. It further held that the 
appellants were liable for suitable punishment under 
the provisions of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971. 
The High Court, however, observed that before passing 
any further order of punishment, it would give one 
additional opportunity to the appellants -judgment 
debtors to comply. The matter was accordingly placed 
for further orders for framing of charge, and the 
appellants were directed to remain personally present 
before the Court. The matter was thereafter listed on 
11th January 2024. 
3.13. Aggrieved by the said order, the appellants are before 
us. 
4. We have heard Mr. Iqbal Syed, learned senior counsel 
appearing for the appellants, and Mr. Nikhil Goel, learned 
senior counsel appearing for the respondents. 
5. This Court, vide interim order dated 11 th January 2024, 
issued notice to the respondents and stayed the 
impugned order passed by the High Court. 
6. Mr. Syed, learned senior counsel appearing for the 
appellants, submitted that the High Court failed to 
appreciate that the conditions imposed by it in the order 
dated 20 th December 2022 were conditions attached to 
the stay granted on the decree pending the first appeal 
and were not independent directions. Therefore, non -
compliance with the said conditions would not amount to 
contempt. At the highest, such non -compliance woul d 

## Page 67

CA @ SLP (C) NO. 963/2024  6 
 
render the stay non-operational or result in its vacation, 
leaving the respondents at liberty to initiate execution 
proceedings. It was, therefore, submitted that the 
contempt proceedings before the High Court were not 
maintainable. In view of the alternative remedy available 
to the respondents by way of execution proceedings, 
learned counsel prayed that this Court set aside the 
impugned order and close the contempt proceedings. 
7. Per contra, Mr. Goel, learned senior counsel appearing for 
the respondents, submitted that there was no infirmity in 
the impugned order passed by the High Court. He 
submitted that once the appellants had given an 
undertaking to deposit the aforesaid amount  and 
obtained the stay pursuant to the order dated 20 th 
December 2022, they were bound to comply with the 
same. It was submitted that the appellants had 
deliberately failed to comply with the order of the High 
Court and, therefore, there was no reason for this Court 
to interfere with the impugned order. 
8. We have considered the rival submissions. Even 
assuming that there was non -compliance with the order 
dated 20 th December 2022, what the High Court had 
granted was a stay of the decree subject to certain 
conditions. The deposit of the decretal amount and costs 
was a condition attached to the stay. Therefore, if the 
appellants did not comply with the conditions, the 
consequence was that the stay would not operate or 

## Page 68

CA @ SLP (C) NO. 963/2024  7 
 
would stand vacated. Such non -compliance, by itself, 
would not amount to wilful disobedience so as to attract 
contempt proceedings. 
9. There is, however, an additional aspect which requires 
consideration. The High Court, in the impugned order, 
has proceeded on the basis that the appellants had 
disobeyed the order dated 20 th December 2022 despite 
having filed an undertaking to deposit the entire decretal 
amount. The said premise, however, is not borne out from 
the record. The undertaking referred to by the High 
Court, whereby the appellants are stated to have 
undertaken to de posit the entire decretal amount, was 
never filed by the present appellants.  
10. On perusal of the affidavit-in-reply dated 20th July 2023, 
filed by appellant no. 1 -judgment debtor in Civil 
Application (for Breach of Order) No. 1 of 2023 in First 
Appeal No. 1138 of 2022, it is evident that, in paragraph 
5 thereof, appellant no. 1 had stated that he was ready 
and willing to deposit an amount of  Rs. 50,00,000/ - 
(Rupees Fifty Lakhs only). The said statement, however, 
was expressly conditional upon the respondent -decree 
holders withdrawing the contempt application. Thus, the 
statement made in the affidavit cannot be construed as 
an unconditional un dertaking to deposit the entire 
decretal amount of Rs. 2,54,00,000/ - (Rupees Two 
Crores, Fifty Four Lakhs only) along with the costs. 

## Page 69

CA @ SLP (C) NO. 963/2024  8 
 
11. Consequently, the finding of the High Court that the 
appellants had failed to comply with an undertaking to 
deposit the entire decretal amount is based on a factual 
premise which is not borne out from the record. In the 
absence of any such undertaking by t he appellants, the 
question of wilful disobedience of such an undertaking 
does not arise. 
12. The respondent -decree holders had, in any event, an 
alternate remedy available to them. Once the conditions 
for the stay were not complied with, they were at liberty 
to take steps for execution of the decree in accordance 
with law. This was the appropriate remedy for recovery of 
the decretal amount. The existence of such a remedy also 
shows why the present contempt proceedings cannot be 
maintained merely on account of non -payment of the 
amount stipulated as a condition for the stay. 
13. The appellants have also stated that they do not have the 
financial capacity to deposit the decretal amount. 
Whether that assertion is correct or not is not required to 
be decided in the present proceedings. The respondent -
decree holders can raise all their claims and seek recovery 
of the decretal amount in execution proceedings in 
accordance with law. 
14. In these circumstances, we are of the view that the 
contempt proceedings initiated against the appellants are 
not maintainable. The High Court erred  in treating the 

## Page 70

CA @ SLP (C) NO. 963/2024  9 
 
non-compliance with the conditions attached to the stay 
as wilful disobedience warranting contempt proceedings. 
15. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed. The impugned order 
passed by the High Court is set aside. The contempt 
proceedings are closed. 
16. It would, however, be open to the respondent(s) -decree 
holder(s) to execute the decree in accordance with law. 
17. Pending applications, if any, to be disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
CIVIL APPEAL NO.6923/2021
1. An additional affidavit has been filed on behalf of the
home buyers in which it is stated that despite direction of
this Court dated 19.09.2025 to handover units within 60
days, the first respondent has failed to handover physical
possession of flats to numerous buyers despite having
received the entire payment a year ago. List of those home
buyers has been annexed as Annexure ‘A’ to the affidavit.
It has also been alleged that the first respondent is
guilty of diverting funds and resources to launch a new
project of which details are provided in paragraph 3.  In
paragraph 4, it is stated that the podium of the project is
not yet complete and there is absolutely no connectivity to
3

## Page 86

Tower ‘H’.  In paragraph 5, it is stated that lifts are not
maintained and in Towers ‘G’ and ‘H’ only two lifts are
operational. Besides, even though two generator sets are
provided only one is functioning.  In paragraph 6, it is
stated that the first respondent had collected Rs.2.5
crores towards Club House Amenities but those amenities are
yet to be provided, and they remain non-functional till
date.  In paragraph 7 of the affidavit, it is stated that
since there has been default on the part of the first
respondent in completing the project and handing over
possession in terms of the allotment, the buyers are
entitled to delay compensation.
2. In view of the aforesaid allegations made in the affidavit
filed on behalf of home buyers, we deem it appropriate to
require  the  first  respondent  to  file  a  comprehensive
affidavit  disclosing:  (a)  Whether  the  possession  of
completed units of which payments have been received has
been provided to the home buyers mentioned in the list
(Annexure  A  to  the  affidavit);  if  not,  why  delay
compensation be not levied upon the first respondent and
awarded to those home buyers who had made full payment and
had completed the necessary formalities on their part. (b)
Whether the podium, as promised at the time of launching
the project, has been completed or not; if not, why it was
not completed.
3. List the matter on 02.09.2026 along with all connected
4

## Page 87

matters including contempt petitions. By the next date,
affidavit shall be filed dealing with the above aspects.
4. By the next date, Greater NOIDA may also file an affidavit
disclosing the amounts and the heads under which it has
raised demand(s) on the project proponent.
Diary No.48524/2025
5. Permission to file SLP is granted.
6. Delay condoned.
7. The learned counsel for the petitioner is permitted to take
steps to file spare copies within 72 hours.  Subject to
filing  of  spare  copies,  issue  notice,  returnable  on
02.09.2026. 
8. Personal appearance of the alleged contemnor(s) is not
required at this stage, provided they are represented by
their counsel(s). 
  (KAVITA PAHUJA)                               (SAPNA BANSAL)
ASTT. REGISTRAR-cum-PS                        COURT MASTER (NSH)

                             O R D E R
1. The matter was taken up for further hearing to report
due compliance of various directions issued by this Court
over a period of time and also to consider some suggestions
at the end of the learned Amicus.
2. In the course of today’s hearing, the learned Amicus
laid much stress and emphasis on constituting a Committee
comprising  of  two  members  of  a  CSO,  experienced  in
rehabilitating the trafficked and have been associated with
the Government and a Bureaucrat serving or retired, with
experience in financial planning for the Government. She
also  laid  emphasis  on  the  fact  that  a  Committee  be
constituted to prepare a SOP for prevention and prosecution
of  cases  of  trafficking  arising  out  of  the  Assisted
Reproductive  Technology  (for  short,  “the  ART”)  and
Surrogacy  Clinics  especially  for  implementing  the
provisions of Section 5(c) and (d) of the ART Act.
3. It is the suggestion of the learned Amicus that the
Committee may be headed by a Retired Judge of this Court
and must include a Medical doctor, preferably a senior
Obstetrician,  experienced  in  IVF  technology,  a  senior
police officer and a lawyer/social worker familiar with
dealing with cases of trafficking.
7

## Page 100

4. As we have been able to understand from what the
learned Amicus has submitted is that when trafficking takes
place, it is the Home Department that gets into action.
However, something needs to be done even at the instance of
the Health Ministry.
5. In the aforesaid context, the learned Amicus has put
forward some of her suggestions in writing as well as the
order passed by this Court dated 27.05.2026.
6. We request Ms. Archana Pathak Dave, the learned A.S.G
to  look  into  the  suggestions  and  also  speak  to  the
authorities  concerned  insofar  as  this  suggestion  of
constituting a Committee referred to above is concerned. We
also request Ms. Dave to get in touch with the Ministry of
Women and Child Development.
7. We also take notice of the status report which has
been filed on behalf of the Ministry of Health and Family
Welfare, Union of India, highlighting in what manner the
provisions  of  the  Assisted  Reproductive  Technology
(Regulation) Act, 2021 (for short, “the Act, 2021”) are
being implemented.
8. We may also say that the Committee constituted by this
Court, headed by Justice Mukta Gupta, former Judge of Delhi
High Court, of which both, the learned Amicus and Ms.
Archana Pathak Dave are Members may also look into the
issues relating to ART 2021 and the Surrogacy Clinics, more
particularly,  for  effective  implementation  of  the
provisions of Section 5 (c) and (d) of the Act and checking
8

## Page 101

of Health and Family Welfare shall also be a part of this
Committee.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Civil Appeal No.11277 of 2026
(@ Special Leave Petition (C) No.33594 of 2025)
M/s G.R. Infra Projects Limited Ratlam
…. Appellant
Versus
The State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors.
…. Respondents
O R D E R
Leave granted.
2. We are, in this appeal, concerned with the Show Cause Notice
(SCN) issued by the respondent-department for the assessment year
2018-19 dated 13.06.2025. The question arising is as to whether the
notice can be one deemed to have been issued under Section 74 of
the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 (CGST Act) read with
Madhya Pradesh Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 (MPGST Act).
3. The assessee, who is the appellant herein, would submit that a
notice issued under Section 74 can only be issued when there is a
fraud/  willful  misstatement/  suppression  of  facts  alleged;  which
allegation has to come out from the notice itself. 
4. Learned Counsel appearing for the appellant submits that the
SCN is beyond the time of three years provided under Section 73 for
1

## Page 112

determination of tax inter alia short paid, for any reason other than
fraud,  willful  misstatement  or  suppression  of  facts.  The  learned
Government Advocate, however, attempts to take us through the
counter affidavit in which according to him the allegations of fraud
and  suppression  of  facts  have  been  elaborated,  justifying  the
proceedings under Section 74 and not under Section 73. 
5. We refused to look at the counter affidavit on the trite principle
that  when  an  authority  has  issued  a  notice  or  an  order,  the
requirements to make the notice or order valid should be contained
in such notice or order and cannot be supplanted by a counter
affidavit in Court, where the notice or order is alleged to be invalid
for reason to non-application of mind, the requirements having not
met and so on and so forth.
6. As far as the CGST Act is concerned, sub-section (2) of Section
73 mandates that the proper officer shall issue notice under sub-
section (1) at least three months prior to the time limit specified in
sub-section (10). Sub-section (10) provides that the proper officer
shall issue the order under Section 9 within three days from the due
date for furnishing of annual return for the financial year relevant to
such  proceedings.  Sub-section  (1)  of  Section  44  provides  for
furnishing an annual return within such time and in such form and in
2

## Page 113

such manner as is prescribed. Rule 80 of the CGST Rules prescribes
the  furnishing  of  an  annual  return  for  every  financial  year  as
specified under Section 44 electronically on or before the 31 st day of
December following the end of such financial year. Hence, for the
relevant assessment year 2018-2019, the annual returns were to be
filed on or before 31.12.2019.
7. The CGST Act came into force on 01.07.2017 and initially for
reason of fresh introduction of the electronic systems, the last date
for filing annual returns was extended for the years commencing
from  2017-2018  onwards  by  notifications  issued  under  Section
44(1).  Insofar  as  the  assessment  year  2018-2019  is  concerned,
successive notifications, extended the time to furnish annual return
and eventually  it  stood at  31.12.2020.  Hence,  the  limitation  for
issuing a notice under Section 73 expires on 31.12.2023. 
8. In the meanwhile, COVID struck and this Court in Writ Petition
(C)  No.3/2020 registered as  Re:  Cognizance  for  Extension  of
Limitation extended  the  limitation  as  provided  in  the  various
statutes, in the wake of the pandemic and eventually by order dated
01.01.2022,  the  Suo  Motu  Writ  Petition  was  disposed  of  with
directions,  inter alia providing for exclusion of limitation for the
period  between  15.03.2020  to  28.02.2022.  While  computing
3

## Page 114

limitation,  the  period  excluded  by  this  Court  coming  within  the
three-year period for 2018-2019 is 1 year and 2 months, which has
to be excluded and further time provided from 31.12.2023 in lieu of
the excluded period. Hence, the extended period of limitation falls
on 28.02.2025. The SCN issued in this case on 13.06.2025 for the
assessment  year  2018-2019  definitely  hit  by  limitation  under
Section 73. Now the question is as to whether Section 74 can be
invoked.
9. The present proceedings were initiated by summons issued
dated 03.03.202 relating to the business for the years 2017-2018 to
2020-2021. From the counter affidavit filed by the State, it is seen
that the petitioner sought time initially, but did not produce the
required documents before the assessing officer. An inspection was
conducted in the premises of the assessee and statements were
recorded  from  the  Accountant,  Authorized  Signatory  and  the
Director of the assessee on various dates. It is alleged that in the
very many hearings scheduled between 01.09.2022 and 07.02.2025;
on 20 occasions, the assessee did not appear. A draft notice-cum-
investigation  report  dated  03.03.2025  was  prepared  and  an
intimation under Section 142 (1A) dated 29.04.2025 was issued to
the  petitioner.  The  petitioner  raised  preliminary  objections  by
response dated 14.05.2025 specifically pointing out that the draft
4

## Page 115

notice has not been served on them. The draft notice was served on
27.05.2025 based on which additional response was submitted by
the petitioner. It was later that SCN dated 13.06.2025 was issued
under Section 74.
10. A bare reading of the notice would indicate that but for a bland
statement of ‘ fraud or concealment of facts ’ nothing is stated as to
how fraud was inferred or concealment of facts were detected. In
fact, the ‘or’ employed indicates that even the assessing officer was
not sure that the assessment was proceeded by reason of fraud or
on the ground of concealment of facts. What is required for the
extended time to be applied are the allegations, which lead to the
inference  of  a  fraud  or  the  concealment  as  attempted  by  the
assessee resulting in suppression of facts, should emanate from the
notice itself. It cannot be a mechanical use of the words ‘fraud,
willful misstatement or suppression of facts’ without listing out the
aspects which persuades the assessing officer to conclude that there
has been employed either of these surreptitious devices by the
assessee.
11. We find absolutely no reason to sustain the SCN issued and find
the High Court to have erroneously upheld the same. We set aside
the impugned order as also the SCN and direct the respondent-State
5

## Page 116

to desist from taking any further proceedings in pursuance of the
SCN challenged before the High Court, which is set aside by this
order.
12. The Civil Appeal stands allowed.
13. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. I.A. No.163222/2026 is allowed.
3. Heard the learned counsels appearing for both the
parties including the learned counsel appearing for the
intervenor.
4. The present matter arises from a dispute relating to
1

## Page 120

agricultural  land  between  close  relatives  regarding
possession and cultivation. The appellant alleges that the
complainant – Harbans and his family members were
attempting to forcibly retain and control over the land
belonging to the appellant’s branch of the family. According
to the appellant, on 22.01.2026, the complainant – Harbans
alongwith Premchand and Samandari, trespassed into the
appellant’s house, locked the house and assaulted him with
lathi, dumbell and knife and attempted to use country-
made pistol and he claims to have acted only in aid of his
private defense. Whereas in the complaint lodged in FIR
No.14/2026 (the present one) against the appellant, it is
alleged that the appellant herein attacked him with knife
and as a retaliatory and counterblast to FIR No.14/2026
lodged by complainant – Harbans, FIR No.15/2026 had
been registered. Apprehending his arrest, the application
for anticipatory bail was filed before the Sessions Court
which came to be rejected and the High Court also affirmed
the same on account of gravity of allegation and opining
custodial interrogation of appellant was warranted. 
2

## Page 121

5. Having heard the learned counsels appearing for the
parties, we notice that there is no dispute with regard to
the fact that both the complainant and the appellant are
closely related. The dispute has arisen with reference to
the agriculture land.
6. Learned counsel appearing for the intervenor would
vehemently oppose grant of bail on the ground that
Harbans had sustained ten injuries on face, neck, shoulder
and it is his contention that he has received the telephonic
threat calls from appellant to withdraw the FIR and he
apprehends danger to his life.
7. Having regard to the relationship between the parties
and no material having been placed by the intervenor to
demonstrate that on receipt of such threat calls, any
complaint having been lodged, we are of the considered
view that appellant would be entitled for being released on
anticipatory bail. We also take note of the fact that in the
complaint lodged by the appellant which culminated in
registration  of  FIR  No.15/2026,  the  accused  persons,
namely, the complainant in FIR No.14/2026 and two others
3

## Page 122

have already been granted bail as an additional ground for
accepting the plea of the appellant in the instant case. It
would not be out of context to refer to the injuries
sustained by the appellant also which are seven in
numbers and it is the case of the appellant that on account
of the assault made by Harbans, who is the complainant in
FIR No.14/2026, he had sustained injuries. This would only
indicate that both the parties being relatives are fighting
for ownership of agricultural land and there being cross
FIRs are all facts which have persuaded us to grant the
relief.  Hence, for the reasons aforestated, we allow this
appeal, set aside the impugned order and direct that the
appellant  be  released  on  anticipatory  bail  by  the
jurisdictional Investigating Officer on such terms and
conditions including the condition of directing him to
appear on every Monday, Friday and Sunday between
11:00 a.m. to 01:00 p.m. and mark his attendance before
the  jurisdictional  police  and  cooperate  with  the
investigation and also on the condition that he shall appear
before the trial court on all the dates of hearing without fail
4

## Page 123

except  when  exempted  specifically  and  such  other
conditions as the Investigating Officer deems fit to impose.

records.

O R D E R
1. Leave granted. 
2. These  appeals  by  way  of  special  leave  arise  out  of  an
interlocutory application filed by the appellants/defendants before the
Trial  Court  for  interim  injunction.  On  28.10.2025,  the  Trial  Court
dismissed  the  interlocutory  application.  However,  by  the  order
impugned  before  us,  the  High  Court  allowed  the  interlocutory
application and directed as under:
"16. The Court is only required to determine the existence of
1

## Page 127

a prima facie case at the stage of considering the application
under Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2 of The Code of Civil
Procedure, 1908 as opposed to examining complex questions
of law or fact. 'Prima facie case' means a substantial question
raised bona fide which needs investigation and a decision on
merits. The Court, at the initial stage, cannot insist upon a
foolproof case warranting an eventual decree1,
17. In this case, there is substance in the argument that title
vests with the appellants since there is no transfer of title to
the Trust (Jamia Elahia) through any Registered Deed. The
Trial Court should also have noticed the other crucial fact of
the objectives of the Trust as of 04.08.2023 being described
as charitable in nature whereas within 13 days of the
registration of the Trust on 17.08.2023, the Trust registered a
DAGPA in favour of the respondents/respondent No.11 for
commercial/real estate purposes.
18. The above reasons constrain us to hold that the Trial
Court failed to notice the suspicious circumstances and the
obvious red flags which the appellants brought to the notice
of  the  Trial  Court.  The  documents  and  circumstances
involved serious questions to be tried. Hence, the Trial Court
ought to have preserved the suit property from being
alienated to third parties till these questions were adjudicated
at  the  time  of  trial.  Suspicious  circumstances,  if  left
unresolved and to the benefit of the contesting respondents,
has the potential to a situation where the plaintiff's rights may
forever be frustrated and the Suit rendered infructuous.
Preservation of the subject property would be crucial in such
a situation to prevent any irreparable prejudice to the
plaintiffs/petitioners (the appellants in this case).
19. To conclude, the impugned order does not disclose a
clear flow of title from the Sale Deeds of 1984 through the
mutation proceedings of 2006 to the creation of the Trust in
2023 in favour of the respondents. Therefore, the Trial Court
erred in holding that the appellants were unable to establish a
prima facie case, balance of convenience and irreparable
injury  for  grant  of  interim  injunction  restraining  the
respondents/defendants  from  creating  third  party
rights/alienating the suit schedule property pending disposal
of the Suit.
1 M/s. Gujarat Bottling Co. Ltd. V. Coca Cola Co., (1995) 5 SCC 545
2

20. CMA No.60 of 2026 is accordingly allowed and disposed
of by setting aside the impugned order dated 28.10.2025.
21. All connected applications are disposed of. Interim orders,
if any, shall stand vacated."

O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. There is a specific stand taken before us that the
appellants are at Sr. No.112, 113, 114 of the merit list.
The advertised posts were 114. The appellants could not be
appointed as, meanwhile, the High Court accepted the claim
of over-aged candidates and directed to accommodate them
over and above the appellants.
1

## Page 134

4. Taking notice of the fact that there is already a
continuous deficiency in the cadre of judicial officers, we
do not see any legal necessity to disturb the order for the
appointment of over-aged candidates. At the same time, we
are of the view that if the appellants were actually at
merit number 112, 113, and 114, they too are entitled to be
accommodated.
5. Consequently and invoking our powers under Article 142
of the Constitution, we dispose of these appeals and
clarify the impugned judgment of the High Court in the
following terms:
(i) The Maharashtra State Public Service Commission is
directed to verify the merit position of the appellants and
consequently make recommendations for appointment of the
candidates at Sr. Nos. 112 to 114 in order of merit. The
needful shall be done within one week; and
(ii) On receipt of these recommendations, the High Court of
Judicature at Bombay and the State of Maharashtra are
directed to take necessary steps and offer appointment to
the said appellants/candidates within two weeks of the
recommendations, subject to such verification as may be
required under the rules. 
6. The interim stay granted on 30.10.2025 also stands
vacated and modified. The over-aged candidates, who were
successful before the High Court, shall also be appointed
2

## Page 135

along with the appellants as per their merits.
7. On appointment, the seniority shall be determined on
the basis of inter se  merit among the various appointees,
irrespective of the fact that any one of them was over-
aged.
8. If so required, the State Government is directed to
sanction additional posts to accommodate the appellants as
well as the over-aged candidates, who were successful
before the High Court.
9. The cases of other over-aged candidates, which are
statedly pending before the High Court, shall be decided as
per their own merits.
10. The  larger  question  of  law  raised  through  these
appeals is kept open.
11. In view of the above, the appeals are disposed of.

     UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. It is brought to our notice that pursuant to our order
dated 03.06.2026, 437 candidates had undertaken the physical
endurance  test  yesterday  i.e.  20.08.2026.  Also,  the
preparation  and  finalization  of  list  qua  125  persons
(approximately), who are to undertake their endurance test
today i.e. 21.08.2026, is under process.
2. We are of the considered view and direct that all of the
candidates need to be confirmed as deemed to have been
qualified the test.  This we say so, as we find that the
criteria laid down vide communication dated 31.07.2026 not to
be in consonance with our order dated 03.06.2026.
3. As  such,  we  direct  the  State/Respondent(s)  to
immediately complete the process of appointment within four
weeks from today. Also, their letters of appointment shall
positively be issued within the said period.
4. Needless to add, all candidates shall complete their
formalities required for authentication of their documents.
5. Mr. P.S. Patwalia and Mr. Sudhanshu S. Chaudhary, learned
senior counsel, submit that such of those home guards who are
gainfully employed with the State for the last fifteen years 
4

## Page 148

have preferred Special Leave Petitions being SLP(C)No. 27022-
27047 of 2024 and SLP ( C) No. 1053-1069/2025. In all, there
are 300 (approximate) petitioners. We are of the considered
view that even these persons can be easily accommodated for
the reason that not only there are vacancies, but all of them,
in fact, have been satisfactorily serving the institution;
also, their initial process of selection and appointment
cannot be disputed.  Since they have been officiating, we see
no reason as to why, they were at the first instance, called
upon to undertake the written test. Ordered accordingly. 
6. We clarify that our directions are confined only to the
original writ petitioners.
7. Also, this order stands passed in the peculiar facts of
this case, not to be treated as a binding precedent.
8. We further clarify that this order shall not govern any
one of the candidates who have sought intervention in any one
of the aforesaid proceedings referred to in Para 5 above.
9. In view of the above directions, we dispose of the present
special leave petitions.
10. All pending application(s) shall also stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NOS.          /2026
[@ SLP [C] NOS.20329-20331/2024]
RAMANKUTTY                            Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
NARAYANANKUTTY & ORS.                 Respondent(s)
O R D E R
Leave granted.
The present appeals have been filed assailing
the impugned judgment dated 17.02.2023 passed by the
High Court of Kerala, wherein, the First Appeals
preferred by the appellant were dismissed.  The first
appeals were filed assailing the common decree and
judgment rendered on 25.02.2006 in O.S. No. 79/1997,
178/1999 and 106/2002.  The three suits were jointly
tried before the Trial Court.  The appellant filed
O.S. No.79/1997, seeking relief of partition of the
suit schedule properties, which was decreed in part.
The second suit being O.S. No.178/1999 was filed
seeking to declare the Settlement Deed No.2939/1997
and Sale Deed No. 2938/1997 as null and void, by the
father of the appellant.  The same came to be
dismissed holding that the aforesaid deeds are not
liable to be declared void. The third suit being O.S.
106/2002  was  filed  seeking  relief  of  permanent

## Page 167

2
prohibitory  injunction  from  trespassing  upon
properties covered by the settlement and assignment
deeds and from obstructing the plaintiff therein i.e.
respondent Nos. 1 and 4 to possess their properties.
The third suit was decreed in favour of respondent
Nos. 1 to 4. The High Court affirmed the findings
rendered by the Trial Court in the three suits and
dismissed the appeals preferred by the appellant vide
the  impugned  order.  Aggrieved  by  the  same,  the
appellant is before this Court.
We have heard the learned counsel appearing for
the parties.
The short issue for consideration in the present
appeals is whether the impugned judgment would be
sustainable in the eyes of law, having been rendered
without taking note of the parameters laid down under
Section 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (for
short, ‘CPC’).
On a perusal of the impugned judgment, we find
that the issues have neither been taken note of nor
answered by the High Court.  The First Appellate
Court is the final Court of facts and law. 
In our considered view, the High Court has not
adverted to the issues raised, pleadings and the
evidence available on record and, thereafter, has not
rendered the judgment by either accepting the views
rendered by the Trial Court, or by reversing it.

## Page 168

3
In such view of the matter, we set aside the
impugned order by remitting it to the High Court for
fresh consideration and to pass a judgment on all the
issues involved and raised before it, in accordance
with Section 96 of the CPC, including the issue of
maintainability.
The appeals stand allowed, accordingly.
Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The above case projects the failure of the judicial system,
when a crime went unpunished and the accused were put to the
torture of a prolonged trial of 22 years and then after conviction,
the appeal filed having been dismissed after yet another 2 decades
and 2 years. The crime, which was committed in the year 1981, was a
double murder. Six accused were arrayed, of which two died before

## Page 191

2
the framing of the charges and three of the four convicted, died
while the appeal was pending before the High Court. The sole
remaining  accused,  aged  about  70  and  troubled  with  multiple
ailments,  has  surrendered  into  custody  after  the  High  Court
convicted him. Altogether, he has spent only 2 years, 4 months and
12 days in custody; hence the crime went unpunished.
2. Despite the horrendous crime of a double murder, we cannot
close our eyes to the ordeal suffered by the accused in the last 45
years. Especially noting his medical condition and the affidavit of
the State that the petitioner is admitted in the hospital, though
in custody, we suspend the sentence and direct that the petitioner
shall be released forthwith on condition of his not committing any
crime when on bail and on his personal surety.
3. In the meantime, let the original record be requisitioned in
the physical as well as digital form with a request to the High
Court\Trial Court to send it within four weeks. Upon receipt of the
records, the soft copy of the same be made available to the learned
counsel for the respective parties as per the procedure adopted by
the Registry.
4. By our earlier order, we had also directed the High Court to
give us a comprehensive Report as to why the trial and the disposal
of the Criminal Appeal was delayed to such an extent. An affidavit
has been filed by the Registrar General of the High Court, which
reveals a shocking pendency of criminal appeals. The delay in trial
was explained with the submission that the accused were absconding
for 6 years but there is no explanation for the 12 years, it took
for the trial to be completed when the charges were framed in the
year 1991. We also notice from the Report of the District and Ses -
sions Judge that the case was transferred from one Court to an -
other, five times in the 11 years after the charge was framed.
5. We were concerned with the pendency of the Criminal Appeals as
pointed out in the Report of the High Court and we hence thought it
fit to permit the petitioner to implead the Union of India in the
above matter. The learned Advocate-on-Record appearing for the High

## Page 192

3
Court would serve a copy of the Affidavit of Compliance filed by
the Registrar General to the Office of the Attorney General/
Solicitor General.
6. The matter shall be posted on 18.09.2026.

        UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The applicant, original petitioner, namely Preeti Singh,
has preferred this Miscellaneous Application praying for the
following:-
“I. Allow this Interlocutory Application and modify the order
dated 31.10.2025 passed by this Hon’ble Court to the extent that
the petitioner shall not effect any development on the remaining
2/3rd part of the suit property should be modified to 1/3rd part
of the Suit property;
II. Pending a final decision in this application, the order
dated 31.10.2025 be kept in abeyance; and/or
III. Pass such other orders as this Hon’ble Court may deem just,
fit and proper in circumstances of the case and interest  of
justice.”
2. We have no hesitation in saying that this application is
thoroughly misconceived. In fact, it is a very misleading
application. 
3. We first take notice of the Order dated 14th December,
2022. 
4. The same reads thus:-
“Issue notice, returnable in six weeks. 
Mr. K. Parameshwar, learned counsel, appears and accepts notice
for the respondent(s)/caveator(s). 
Until further orders, there shall be stay of the impugned order
passed by the High Court on the condition that the petitioner
files an undertaking on an affidavit that she will keep 1/3rd
portion of the property in question intact, as claimed by the
plaintiff in the plaint, and will not make any construction
thereon.”
5. We also take notice of the order dated 31st October,
2022, of whose clarification is sought for by way of the
present application.

## Page 200

3
6. The same reads thus:
“1. The present petition has been filed against the
judgment and order dated 24.09.2022 passed by the learned
Single Judge of the High Court, whereby the High Court has
allowed the Appeal.
2. The Trial Court had rejected the application for
injunction. The same was carried in appeal.
3. The High Court in appeal found that it was necessary to
preserve the property during the pendency of the suit.
4. A perusal of the material on record would reveal that
the claim of Respondent Nos.1 and 3 is with regard to
1/3rd share each in the suit property, which, according to
them originally belonged to their father.
5. It is the contention of the learned senior counsels
appearing for Respondent Nos. 1 and 3 that the share of
respondent No.2, who is their brother, would at the most
be restricted to 1/3rd of the suit property.
6. In that view of the matter, we dispose of this petition
by  directing  that  the  petitioner  shall  restrict  the
development of property only to the 1/3rd part of the suit
property. The petitioner shall not effect any development
on the remaining 2/3rd part of the suit property.
7. The learned Trial Court is requested to decide the suit
expeditiously.
8. Needless to state that the learned Trial Judge would
not be influenced by the observation made by the learned
Single Judge of the High Court in the impugned order.
9. The special leave petition is, accordingly, disposed
of.”
7. By Order dated 14th December 2022, this Court had made itself
very clear that the petitioner shall file an undertaking that she
would keep 1/3rd portion of the property in question intact, more
particularly, when she knew that there are two more sharers in the
property. In fact, in law, she has only 1/3rd share in the subject
property. 
8. On 31st October, 2025, when the petition came to be disposed
of, this Court observed that the petitioner shall restrict the
development of property only to 1/3rd of the suit property. This
Court had made itself very clear that the petitioner shall not
effect any development on the remaining 2/3rd  part of the suit

property. Today, the petitioner comes before us and says that she

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.   6827 OF 2018  
EX. CADET MOHIT KUMAR JAKHAR APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
UNION OF INDIA & ORS.     RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. The present case is a very unfortunate case of a
cadet, i.e., the appellant herein, who unfortunately, could
not complete the four-year course at the Indian Naval
Academy, Ezhimala, Kannur, Kerala. He was selected as a
Training Cadet at the Indian Naval Academy, Ezhimala,
Kannur, Kerala, but could not complete the 8 th semester
course in its entirety.
2. It  is  noteworthy  to  mention  here  that,  upon
successful completion of the course, in terms of the
agreement between the Ministry of Defence and Jawaharlal
Nehru University, and the Ordinance governing the field, a
degree of Bachelor of Engineering is awarded by Jawaharlal
Nehru University. However, Ordinance 34 makes it clear that
a candidate is required to pass all the prescribed courses
as laid down therein.
1

## Page 203

3. The petitioner himself has admitted in the writ
petition that he was unable to complete the entire 8 th
semester course.
4. The reply filed by the respondent–Union of India, as
well as by Jawaharlal Nehru University, makes it clear that
they have no objection in furnishing the mark sheets up to
the 7 th semester, thereby enabling the student to seek
admission  to  the  8 th semester  in  any  other
university/institution  in  the  country  offering  an
equivalent course.
5. In view of the aforesaid circumstances, the present
appeal  stands  disposed  of  with  a  direction  to  the
respondent–Union of India to release all certificates,
including the mark sheets, up to the 7 th semester to the
appellant, if the same have not already been released.
6. The university/institution offering a similar or
equivalent course shall grant admission to the appellant to
the 8th semester course, thereby enabling him to complete
the four-year degree course in B.Tech.
7. The delay in the matter of granting admission shall
not come in the way of the appellant in case he seeks
admission  to  the  8 th semester  course  in  any  other
university/institution offering an equivalent course.
8. The appellant is granted two weeks' time to submit a
representation to the Commandant, Indian Naval Academy,
2

## Page 204

Ezhimala, Kannur, Kerala to the said effect. The respondent
shall, within two weeks thereafter, furnish all relevant
and minute details, including the mark sheets up to the 7 th
semester, to the appellant, if the same have not already
been provided, enabling him to seek admission to the 8 th
semester in another university/institution.
9. With the aforesaid observations and directions, the
appeal stands disposed of.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (C) NO.27532 OF 2025
SRI ARUN KUMAR DEY
…. PETITIONER
VERSUS
THE OIL AND NATURAL GAS
CORPORATION LIMITED
(ONGC) THR. ITS EXECUTIVE
DIRECTOR AND ANR.
…. RESPONDENTS
O R D E R
The petitioner was the applicant before the High Court seeking
arbitration with respect to the dispute arising from the execution of
work entrusted by the first respondent. The High Court found that
indeed there was an Arbitration Clause in the agreement between
the parties. However, the High Court, on an examination of the
facts, found that the petitioner had issued many notices and raised
further claims in the subsequent notices finding that this is
impermissible under the Arbitration Clause, thus disentitling the
petitioner to an arbitration as permitted in the agreement.
2. We were definite that the impugned order cannot be sustained;
especially since the Court at the stage of a Section 11 application is
only supposed to look into whether there is an Arbitration Clause or
1

## Page 207

not. Having found an Arbitration Clause, the parties should have
been left to agitate all their contentions before the Arbitrator. The
parties, hence, consented for appointment of an Arbitrator. We
called for suggestions from the parties and based on that we appoint
Hon’ble Justice (Retd.) Shri Subhashis Talapatra, former Chief
Justice, High Court of Orissa (Address: VIP Road, Bangladesh
Assistant High Commission, Near Circuit House, Kunjaban, Agartala,
Tripura – 799 001, Email id:  reachsubhasis@gmail.com, Mobile
No.9436122984) as the sole Arbitrator to adjudicate upon the
disputes that have arisen between the parties.
3. The Arbitrator shall issue notices to the parties in connection
with the arbitral proceedings. He is left free to determine his fee. We
make it clear that we have expressed no opinion on the merits of
the case which aspect is left open for the parties to urge before the
learned Arbitrator. The Registry of this Court shall intimate the
learned Arbitrator. No costs.
4. The special leave petition stands disposed of.
5. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.

O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The appellant challenges the judgment/order dated
30.10.2025 in FAO (OS) No.79 of 2023 passed by the High
Court of Delhi at New Delhi.
3. Having heard learned senior counsel appearing for the
respective parties, we are of the considered view that
the impugned judgment/order dated 30.10.2025 needs to be
quashed and set aside for the same having been passed
without considering the material placed on record.
4. As  such,  without  expressing  any  opinion  on  the
merits, on this short ground alone, we remand the matter
to the High Court for consideration afresh. The impugned
judgment/order dated 30.10.2025 is quashed and set aside.
5. We direct the parties to appear before the High Court
on 28.09.2026.
6. We request the High Court to take up the matter and
decide the same on an expeditious basis.
7. Accordingly, the present appeal stands allowed.

Principal Judge, Family Court, District – Burhanpur, Madhya Pradesh
to the Principal Judge, Family Court, Vijayapur, Karnataka.

Karnataka is about 630 kms.

this Court is of the considered opinion that the present Transfer
Petition deserves to be allowed.

Upon hearing the counsel, the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. We have heard the learned Senior Counsel appearing
for the petitioner and the learned counsel appearing for
1

## Page 262

the respondents. 
2. The petitioner is also present before us.
3. Notice was issued only to facilitate the interaction
of the petitioner with his child.  We are conscious of
the fact that the petitioner had preferred an application
before the Family Court, Morbi, Gujarat, invoking the
provisions of the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, which
has been dismissed for want of jurisdiction.
4. Today, after the order was passed, the petitioner
became very emotional and created a ruckus.  However, we
are inclined to take a lenient view as the emotions have
overtaken the petitioner.
5. The learned counsel appearing for the respondents
repeatedly submitted before this Court that the same
conduct is exhibited whenever there is an interaction.
6. Notwithstanding  what  happened  before  this  Court
today, we are inclined to facilitate the petitioner to
interact with his child.  While doing so, we are quite
conscious of the apprehension expressed by the learned
counsel for the respondents.
7. In such view of the matter, the respondent-mother is
directed to bring the child on the last Saturday of every
month, starting from September, 2026, between 03:00 p.m.
and  06:00  p.m.  before  the  Family  Court,  Ahmedabad,
2

## Page 263

Gujarat.  The Juvenile Justice Board concerned will
ensure that a responsible local Counsellor accompanies
the  mother  of  the  child,  only  for  the  purpose  of
extending  security,  while  she  takes  the  child  for
interaction. Liberty is granted to the Counsellor to have
the assistance of local Police in order to avoid any
untoward incident.
8. We further make it clear that during interaction, the
Counsellor and the mother shall be at a reasonable
distance.   If  during  the  aforesaid  arrangement  any
untoward incident takes place, liberty is granted to the
parties, especially to the respondent(s), to file an
appropriate  application  along  with  a  report  of  the
Juvenile Justice Board before this Court in the event of
non-implementation of this order.
9. This  order  is  passed  without  prejudice  to  the
petitioner to pursue appropriate remedy in the manner
known to law.
10. Accordingly,  the  Special  Leave  Petition  stands
disposed of in the above terms.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.
